Inherited from Old Spanish templo (cf. also the popular variant tiemplo), borrowed from Latin templum, from Proto-Indo-European *t(e)mp-lo-s, from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).
Inherited from Old Spanish, inherited from Latin tingere, from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to soak, dip”).

Inherited from Old Spanish tiempo, from Latin tempus, from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”). Doublet of tempo. Compare both English tempo, temperature.

parole.significato: thrush (kind of bird); species Turdus musicus
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin turdus (“a thrush”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos.
Borrowed from Latin torvus.

parole.significato: to bring (in the sense of transport, for differences with llevar and examples see that entry)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish traer, from Latin trahō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ-.
Inherited from Old Spanish treyenta, from Latin trīgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *tri(d)ḱomt (“thirty”).
From Latin tremere, from Proto-Indo-European *trem- (“tremble”).
Inherited from Old Spanish tronco, from Latin truncus. Cognate with English trunk, Italian tronco, Portuguese tronco.

parole.significato: end, terminus (the terminal point of something in space or time)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin terminus, from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”).
From Latin tumulus (“mound; barrow”), from tumeō (“to swell”), from Proto-Indo-European *tūm- (“to swell, to increase”).
From Latin unguentum (“ointment”), from unguō (“to smear with ointment”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to salve, anoint”).
From Latin urgentem (“urgent”), from urgeō (“to urge”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to work”).

parole.significato: cow (adult female of the species Bos taurus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin vacca.
Inherited from Old Spanish vedar, from Latin vetāre. Doublet of vetar.
Borrowed from Latin vēlōcem.
Inherited from Old Spanish vena, from Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin.
Borrowed from Latin verbum, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”).

Inherited from Old Spanish verga, berga, inherited from Latin virga (“slender green branch, twig, stick”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *wisgeh₂ (“flexible rod or stick”). Compare Portuguese verga. Doublet of verja (“fence”).
Derived from Latin vice (“in place of”), from the ablative of vicis (“alternation, turn”).

parole.significato: seeing person (someone who is not blind)
parole.testo: From Latin videntem (“seeing”), present active participle of videō (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; to see”).
Inherited from Old Spanish vientre, from Latin ventrem (“stomach, belly”), from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-.

Inherited from Latin vīventem, accusative of Latin vīventem, the present active participle of vīvō (“live, be alive”). The same formation, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃wontm̥, is seen in Ashkun źit, Kamkata-viri ǰat, Sanskrit जीवन्त (jī́vanta), Waigali ǰit.
Inherited from Latin volāre. Doublet of volear. Compare Galician and Portuguese voar.
Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, from earlier volva, from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind”).
From Latin vertebra (“joint”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.
Borrowed from Latin victima.
Inherited from Old Spanish yerno, from Latin generum (“son-in-law”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.
Inherited from Latin alid, variant form of aliud, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin anatem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts (“duck”).

Borrowed from Latin asperum, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”).
